items.prompt: What is the outermost layer of Earth?

options.label: The mantle
options.feedback: The mantle lies below the crust, not on the surface.

options.label: The core
options.feedback: The core is at the center of Earth, not the outermost layer.

options.label: The crust
options.feedback: The crust is the thin, outermost layer of Earth.

options.label: The asthenosphere
options.feedback: The asthenosphere is a semi-fluid layer beneath the lithosphere, not the outermost one.

items.ok_line: The crust is the thin outer shell of Earth.
items.ko_line: The crust is the only layer at the surface.
items.exp_text: The crust is the outermost layer of Earth. It is very thin compared to the layers beneath it, ranging from about 5 to 70 kilometers in depth.

items.prompt: Which layer of Earth is liquid?

options.label: The inner core
options.feedback: The inner core is solid, not liquid.

options.label: The outer core
options.feedback: The outer core is a fluid layer made mostly of iron and nickel.

options.label: The mantle
options.feedback: The mantle is solid rock that can flow slowly, but it is not liquid.

options.label: The lithosphere
options.feedback: The lithosphere is rigid and brittle, not liquid.

items.ok_line: The outer core is the only fully liquid layer.
items.ko_line: The outer core is the fluid layer of Earth.
items.exp_text: The outer core is a liquid layer composed mostly of iron and nickel. It sits above the solid inner core and below the mantle.

items.prompt: What are the two main chemical layers of Earth's crust?

options.label: Oceanic and continental
options.feedback: Yes, the crust is divided into denser oceanic crust and less dense continental crust.

options.label: Upper and lower
options.feedback: Upper and lower are divisions of the mantle, not of the crust.

options.label: Sial and sima
options.feedback: Sial and sima are rock types within the crust, but they are not the two main chemical layers.

options.label: Lithosphere and asthenosphere
options.feedback: Those are mechanical layers, not chemical layers of the crust.

items.ok_line: The crust has oceanic and continental parts.
items.ko_line: Oceanic and continental are the two crust types.
items.exp_text: The crust is compositionally divided into oceanic crust, which is thin and dense, and continental crust, which is thicker and less dense. Both are made of silicate minerals but differ in composition.

items.prompt: What is the thickest layer of Earth?

options.label: The crust
options.feedback: The crust is very thin compared to the layers beneath, so it is not the thickest.

options.label: The outer core
options.feedback: The outer core is about 2,260 km thick, but the mantle is much thicker.

options.label: The mantle
options.feedback: The mantle extends to a depth of 2,890 km, making it the thickest layer.

options.label: The inner core
options.feedback: The inner core has a radius of about 1,220 km, far less than the mantle's thickness.

items.ok_line: The mantle is the thickest layer of Earth.
items.exp_text: The mantle is Earth's thickest layer, extending from below the crust down to about 2,890 km depth. It makes up most of Earth's volume.

items.prompt: What is the lithosphere made of?

options.label: Only the crust
options.feedback: The lithosphere includes more than just the crust.

options.label: Only the upper mantle
options.feedback: The lithosphere also includes the crust, not just the upper mantle.

options.label: The entire mantle and the core
options.feedback: The lithosphere is only the outermost rigid shell, not the whole mantle or core.

options.label: The crust and the top of the upper mantle
options.feedback: The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell made of the crust and the very top of the upper mantle.

items.ok_line: It is crust plus the uppermost mantle.
items.ko_line: The lithosphere includes both crust and upper mantle.
items.exp_text: The lithosphere is the rigid, brittle outer shell of Earth. It consists of the crust and the topmost part of the upper mantle, all moving together as tectonic plates.

items.prompt: What is the main chemical composition of Earth's core?

options.label: Silicate minerals
options.feedback: Silicate minerals are found in the crust and mantle, not in the core.

options.label: Iron and nickel
options.feedback: The core is made mostly of iron, with some nickel and light elements.

options.label: Magnesium and silicon
options.feedback: These are common in the mantle, not the core.

options.label: Basalt and granite
options.feedback: Those are types of crustal rock, not core material.

items.ok_line: Iron and nickel dominate the core.
items.ko_line: The core is iron-nickel, not silicate or basalt.
items.exp_text: Earth's core is composed largely of iron, about 80%, along with nickel and some lighter elements. It is the densest part of the planet.

options.label: A semi-fluid layer of the upper mantle
options.feedback: The asthenosphere is a ductile, semi-fluid layer where tectonic plates move.

options.label: The rigid outer shell of Earth
options.feedback: That is the lithosphere, not the asthenosphere.

options.label: The liquid part of the core
options.feedback: The liquid core is the outer core, not the asthenosphere.

options.label: The lower part of the mantle
options.feedback: The lower mantle is called the mesosphere, not the asthenosphere.

items.ok_line: It is a semi-fluid layer under the lithosphere.
items.ko_line: The asthenosphere is semi-fluid, not rigid or liquid core.
items.exp_text: The asthenosphere is a ductile, semi-fluid layer chiefly in the upper mantle. Tectonic plates float and move on top of it.

items.prompt: What is the boundary between the crust and the mantle called?

options.label: The Conrad discontinuity
options.feedback: The Conrad discontinuity is within the crust, not between crust and mantle.

options.label: The transition zone
options.feedback: The transition zone is inside the mantle, not at its top boundary.

options.label: The Mohorovičić discontinuity
options.feedback: The Moho marks the change from crust to mantle, where seismic wave speeds change due to density.

options.label: The core-mantle boundary
options.feedback: That is the boundary between the mantle and the core, not between crust and mantle.

items.ok_line: The Moho separates crust from mantle.
items.ko_line: The Mohorovičić discontinuity is the crust-mantle boundary.
items.exp_text: The Mohorovičić discontinuity, often called the Moho, is the distinct change in seismic wave velocity that marks the boundary between the crust and the mantle. It is caused by a change in rock density.

items.prompt: What is the inner core of Earth like?

options.label: It is liquid and made of iron
options.feedback: The liquid iron layer is the outer core, not the inner core.

options.label: It is a gas under high pressure
options.feedback: The inner core is solid, not gas.

options.label: It is made of silicate rock
options.feedback: Silicate rock is in the crust and mantle, not the core.

options.label: It is a solid ball of iron and nickel
options.feedback: The inner core is solid, composed mostly of iron and nickel.

items.ok_line: It is solid iron and nickel.
items.ko_line: The inner core is solid, not liquid or silicate.
items.exp_text: The inner core is the innermost layer of Earth. It is a solid ball with a radius of about 1,220 km, made primarily of iron and some nickel. It is solid despite being very hot, because of the enormous pressure.

items.prompt: How does the density of the continental crust compare to the oceanic crust?

options.label: It is denser
options.feedback: The oceanic crust is denser, not the continental crust.

options.label: It is less dense
options.feedback: The continental crust is less dense than the oceanic crust.

options.label: They have the same density
options.feedback: They differ: oceanic is denser than continental.

options.label: It varies randomly with no pattern
options.feedback: There is a clear pattern: continental is less dense than oceanic.

items.ok_line: Continental crust is lighter than oceanic.
items.ko_line: Oceanic crust is denser than continental.
items.exp_text: The oceanic crust is dense because it is rich in iron and magnesium silicates, while the continental crust is less dense and richer in feldspar and quartz. This is why continents stand higher than the ocean floor.
